message.reasoning:
I need to decide whether to bid on Kentucky Avenue in this auction.

I own Illinois Avenue, so Kentucky would complete the red set. p4 has $1501 and can bid forever, making a $221 bid too risky. I will drop out.

I am reconsidering. Indiana is still unowned, so the real prize may be a full red set rather than just Kentucky. I also need $333 cash to survive p1's orange houses.

I am checking standard Monopoly rent tables and board positions to evaluate the value of Park Place and Boardwalk.

I mapped the board positions. From North Carolina Avenue, the next seven spaces are Community Chest, Pennsylvania Avenue, Short Line, Chance, Park Place, Luxury Tax, and Boardwalk. I am calculating how often these will be landed on.

p4 owns three railroads, yielding $100 in rent. Winning Kentucky would leave me with only $111 cash. That is too risky because Short Line alone costs $100, and Park Place or Boardwalk would require mortgaging properties. I am weighing the mortgage values of my holdings to see if I could afford the rent.

Liquidating all holdings plus selling houses yields roughly $601. Standard orange rent tables are being checked to see if that covers the rent.

I corrected the orange rent figures. St. James Place, Tennessee Avenue, and New York Avenue each pay $550 for three houses. I had previously misremembered these amounts.

I will trust the standard orange rent values. p1 has only $114 cash, so they cannot build a fourth house on any orange property. If I do not buy Kentucky, I can liquidate my holdings for roughly $823.

Liquidating all holdings still leaves roughly $823, which easily covers even the highest orange rent. Buying Kentucky for $222 would leave about $711 after mortgaging and selling houses. The real question is whether the red monopoly is worth fighting p4's endless one-dollar increments.

If p4 wins Kentucky, they still cannot complete the red set without my Illinois. I would need both Indiana and their property to finish it. Getting Kentucky myself is much easier because I only need Indiana. Denying p4 the bid does not help me finish the set.

A red monopoly would double the rent on each property. Unimproved, that is only a modest gain. With houses, the payoff is severe: Illinois three houses pay $750 and a hotel pays $1100.

Building on red properties costs $150 per house, so cash is tight. p4 will likely raise the bid by one dollar each time to deny me the red set. I am now checking whether p4 could complete other monopolies, such as green or yellow, if I drop out.

p4 cannot complete any other monopoly without a trade. They own two-thirds of yellow and green, but Ventnor blocks yellow and Penn Ave blocks green. They also lack Vermont for light blue. I would hold two-thirds red after winning Kentucky, needing only Indiana to finish the set.

The brown monopoly is already mine but weak. I am now reconsidering whether the $220 list price is the right ceiling, since Kentucky is worth more to me than to p4.

Forcing p4 to pay $300–$400 would drain their cash, but they have $1501 so it barely matters. Winning at $250 would leave only $83, yet I am only eight spaces from GO and could collect $200 in one or two turns. The real risk is that p4 will match any bid with a one-dollar increment, so I cannot stop them from paying whatever price they want.

I cannot know p4's maximum bid, but they will likely pay well above list to stop me from completing the red set. Cash preservation is critical for surviving the orange houses and the Indiana auction. If I drop out, I still own Illinois, which blocks them. However, owning Indiana alone would leave me with only two-thirds of the red set, mirroring their current position.

If I drop out of the Kentucky auction, p4 will own it. I must then fight hard for Indiana to prevent them from completing the red set. A split 2-1 is acceptable, since neither player would hold a full monopoly.

I cannot outbid p4 if they value blocking me more than I value winning. A $222 bid would only start a one-dollar war that drains my cash. I will drop out.

I realized that buying Kentucky for $222 would leave only $111. That is below Indiana's list price of $220, so I could not purchase it even if I wanted to. This makes the auction a dead end.

I cannot reach Indiana this lap. It is 31 spaces away from my current position on North Carolina Avenue, so I would need to pass GO and circle the board before landing there.

p3 is on Kentucky and could land on Indiana next turn with a roll of two. p1 is on St. Charles and would need a twelve to reach it, so that seems unlikely. p4 is in jail.

Mortgaging Ventnor and Penn Avenue could raise enough cash to buy Indiana after winning Kentucky. The red properties would remain unmortgaged and developable.

Mortgaging Ventnor and Penn would still block p4 from completing the yellow and green monopolies, since ownership does not transfer. I will assume I can mortgage properties whenever I need cash to raise funds for the bid.

I am now uncertain whether mortgaging is allowed during an auction. If I bid up to $333, winning at $300 would leave only $33 cash. Dark blue and orange rent hits are likely before I can pass GO. I may need to mortgage immediately.

Rolling a 3 lands on Short Line for $100. A 5 lands on Park Place for $175. A 6 lands on the tax square for $75. A 7 lands on Boardwalk for $200. The chance of hitting any of these before passing GO is roughly 47 percent.

The turn order is p1, p2, p3, p4. After p3's auction turn, p4 will move next while still in jail, then p1, then me. I will not roll for several turns.

I will drop out at $220. p4 will raise the bid by one dollar each turn, so I cannot stop them from winning.

Bidding up only drains the bank, not p4's cash. They have $1501 and can pay any rent regardless. The only way bidding helps is if I win at a price that makes the set worthwhile. p4 has already refused to drop on North Carolina Avenue and Pacific Avenue.

I considered bidding $250 to test p4's maximum, but I rejected the idea. They have $1501 and know the strategic stakes, so they will likely keep raising by one dollar. Overpaying is too risky.

I will drop out of the Kentucky auction. p4 bid $221 exactly as predicted, so I will follow my earlier plan and not raise further. I am drafting a public message that acknowledges they can have the property, notes they still cannot finish the red set without Illinois, and keeps Indiana as the real target. I will avoid sounding desperate or revealing my budget for Indiana.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.
